structure.title: I
structure.summary: In the spring of 1922, Nick Carraway arrives in West Egg and rents a modest eighty-dollar-a-month bungalow, feeling isolated until a stranger asks him for directions to West Egg village, granting him a sense of belonging. He buys twelve volumes on banking and investment securities, aiming to become a 'well-rounded man,' and later drives by car to East Egg to visit his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom, who live in an opulent Georgian Colonial mansion. During dinner, Tom aggressively promotes racist pseudoscience from The Rise of the Coloured Empires, Daisy makes a cynical remark about women being 'beautiful little fools,' and a phone call reveals Tom’s affair with a woman in New York, which Jordan Baker confirms to Nick in hushed tones; Daisy then claims a nightingale sings outside and calls Nick an 'absolute rose' before confiding in him about her daughter’s birth and her disillusionment, smirking as if sharing elite knowledge. That night, after leaving the mansion, Nick sits on an abandoned grass roller in his yard and observes Gatsby standing alone in the shadows of his neighbor’s mansion, trembling as he stretches his arms toward a single green light far across the bay, which vanishes as Gatsby disappears into the darkness.

structure.title: II
structure.summary: On a summer Sunday afternoon, Nick Carraway travels by train with Tom Buchanan from West Egg to New York, stopping at the desolate valley of ashes where Tom forcibly leads him to George Wilson’s garage beneath the looming billboard of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg to meet Myrtle Wilson, Tom’s mistress; they then take separate taxis to New York, with Myrtle purchasing a ten-dollar Airedale dog from a street vendor and stopping at a newsstand for magazines and perfume, before arriving at her top-floor apartment at 158th Street where she hosts a gathering with her sister Catherine and neighbors Mr. and Mrs. McKee; as Tom opens whisky and Nick becomes intoxicated, Myrtle transforms from earthy vitality to theatrical hauteur in a cream chiffon dress, drunkenly insists on saying Daisy’s name, provoking Tom to violently break her nose, while Catherine reveals Myrtle married George believing he was a gentleman and now regrets it, and Mrs. McKee shares her own marital regrets, culminating in chaos as Mr. McKee drifts in and out of consciousness, after which Nick escapes the apartment and finds himself alone in the cold, dimly lit Pennsylvania Station at dawn waiting for a train.

structure.title: III
characters_present: The man who emerged from the wrecked coupé
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway, Nick, receiving a formal invitation to Jay Gatsby’s mansion on Long Island, where he arrives by car after seven p.m. to find an opulent, overcrowded party fueled by champagne, jazz, and guests arriving in Rolls-Royces and station wagons. Amid wild rumors that Gatsby killed a man or was a German spy, Nick wanders through the lavish grounds—observing a library with real books examined by a drunken guest in owl-eyed spectacles, performances by a tenor and contralto, and a chaotic atmosphere that peaks at midnight—until he meets Jordan Baker, who introduces him to Gatsby himself, revealing the host as young and composed, standing apart from the revelry. After Gatsby invites Nick to fly in his hydroplane the next morning and Jordan discloses Gatsby’s claim of attending Oxford (which she doubts), the party descends into drunken chaos: a woman sings while weeping ink-tears, marital fights erupt, and a coupé crashes outside, with Owl Eyes denying he was driving and a second man stumbling out dazedly asking for a gas station, as Nick departs to find Gatsby alone on the porch gesturing farewell under the moon. The chapter closes with Nick reflecting on his summer life in New York—working at the Probity Trust, studying investments at the Yale Club, walking past the Murray Hill Hotel to Pennsylvania Station, and rekindling a connection with Jordan Baker, whom he discovers has lied about damaging a borrowed car and cheated in a golf tournament, yet he remains emotionally detached, declaring himself one of the few honest people he knows.

structure.title: IV
structure.summary: On a Sunday morning in 1922, Gatsby’s mansion hosts an extravagant party filled with dozens of guests from East Egg, West Egg, and New York, including Ripley Snell, Benny McClenahan, Klipspringer, and Henry L. Palmetto, who spread wild rumors about Gatsby’s origins while mingling amid cocktails and flowers; later that summer, Gatsby arrives at Nick Carraway’s door in his cream-colored car with a three-noted horn, invites him to lunch, and recounts an elaborate, inconsistent personal history—including Oxford education, wartime heroism in Europe, and a Montenegrin medal for valor—producing physical proof that momentarily convinces Nick Carraway; during lunch at a cellar restaurant on Forty-second Street, Gatsby introduces Nick Carraway to Meyer Wolfsheim, a grotesque underworld figure who wears cuff buttons made of human molars and reveals that Gatsby fixed the 1919 World Series before vanishing abruptly; in flashback, Jordan Baker recalls encountering Gatsby in 1917 Louisville as a lieutenant courting Daisy Fay, who later married Tom Buchanan after a lavish engagement marked by a $350,000 string of pearls and a drunken emotional breakdown on her wedding day; after leaving the Plaza Hotel, Jordan reveals to Nick Carraway that Gatsby bought his mansion solely to be near Daisy across the bay and seeks a quiet tea invitation through Nick Carraway’s proximity to her home, prompting Nick Carraway to reflect on human roles as he draws Jordan close in a victoria through Central Park at twilight.

structure.title: V
structure.summary: On a late night in West Egg, Nick returns home to find Gatsby’s mansion brilliantly lit and Gatsby approaching him nervously with a confidential business proposition, which Nick declines; the next morning, Nick invites Daisy for tea, warning her not to bring Tom, and on the day of the meeting, heavy rain falls as Gatsby arranges for Nick’s grass to be cut and a greenhouse full of flowers—jonquils, hawthorn, plum blossoms, and kiss-me-at-the-gate—to be delivered. Daisy arrives by large open car with her chauffeur Ferdie, and Gatsby, pale and trembling, nearly collapses upon seeing her; they meet awkwardly in the living room, where Gatsby nearly knocks over a mantel clock, but after a long silence, their tension eases into quiet joy as Gatsby invites them to tour his mansion. They walk through opulent, eerily empty rooms—Marie Antoinette music-rooms, Restoration Salons, period bedrooms—before Gatsby displays his lavish collection of shirts—linen, silk, and flannel in coral, apple-green, lavender, and faint orange—with intricate monograms and patterns, overwhelming Daisy into stormy tears as she buries her face in the fabric; Gatsby watches her with awe, revaluing his possessions through her reaction, and reveals he employs a man in England to send him seasonal clothing. As rain resumes, Gatsby points out the green light at Daisy’s dock, its romantic symbolism now diminished by her physical presence; Nick examines photographs of Dan Cody and a young Gatsby in yachting gear, while Daisy admires his old pompadour and yacht imagery; Gatsby shows newspaper clippings about Daisy, and when Klipspringer is summoned to play piano, his nervous performance of 'The Love Nest' and 'One Thing’s Sure' echoes the storm outside, as Nick observes Gatsby’s growing bewilderment that Daisy cannot fully match his idealized vision, until Gatsby takes her hand and Nick Carraway departs alone into the rain, leaving them completely absorbed in each other.

structure.title: VI
structure.summary: A New York reporter arrives at Gatsby’s West Egg mansion one morning, mistakenly believing him to be a public figure, revealing the wild rumors surrounding him—such as his home being a moving boat or connected to an underground pipeline to Canada. The narrative then shifts to Gatsby’s origin as James Gatz of North Dakota, who at seventeen rowed out to Dan Cody’s yacht anchored off Lake Superior in Little Girl Bay, adopted the name Jay Gatsby during their first conversation, and spent five years aboard the Tuolomee working as steward, jailor, and companion, absorbing wealth and excess while learning to avoid alcohol after witnessing Cody’s drunkenness; after Cody’s death in Boston, Ella Kaye secured his fortune through legal means, leaving Gatsby with no inheritance but a fully formed identity and education. Later, after weeks of absence, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s mansion on a Sunday afternoon and is startled by the unexpected arrival of Tom Buchanan, Mr. Sloane, and a woman in a brown riding-habit on horseback; Gatsby, visibly nervous, insists they stay for drinks and supper, but their aloofness and Sloane’s quiet intervention prevent him from joining their dinner invitation, leaving Gatsby behind in his car as they ride off. Tom and Daisy later attend one of Gatsby’s parties, where Daisy is visibly unsettled by the excess, and Gatsby, dancing with her, confides his desperate hope that she will tell Tom, 'I never loved you,' believing he can repeat the past—a belief rooted in his memory of kissing Daisy under moonlight five years earlier, when he felt his dreams had become real.

structure.title: VII
structure.summary: On the hottest day of summer, Nick arrives by train at the Buchanans’ house to find Gatsby waiting, having replaced his original servants with mysterious relatives of Wolfsheim; during lunch, Daisy openly kisses Gatsby and declares her love, provoking Tom to challenge Gatsby’s claim of Oxford education and expose his bootlegging ties to Meyer Wolfsheim. The group drives to New York in a tense car arrangement—Daisy and Gatsby in the coupé, Tom, Nick, and Jordan in Gatsby’s yellow car—stopping at Wilson’s garage where Wilson, visibly ill, reveals his plan to flee with Myrtle, while Myrtle watches from above, mistaking Jordan for Tom’s wife. At the Plaza Hotel, the confrontation escalates as Daisy admits she once loved Tom but now loves Gatsby, yet refuses to say she never loved Tom; Tom forces them to leave together in Gatsby’s car, while Nick and Jordan depart with Tom, who is triumphant but emotionally detached. Later, Myrtle is struck and killed by a speeding yellow car that flees the scene in the valley of ashes; Michaelis witnesses her desperate cry before the accident and is uncertain of the car’s color, initially describing it as light green. Tom and Nick arrive at the garage to find Wilson in hysterics, mourning Myrtle, and Tom insists his blue coupé was not involved, though he had promised to deliver a new car to Wilson. That night, Gatsby approaches Nick outside the Buchanan mansion, confessing Daisy was driving the fatal car but he will take the blame; Nick finds Tom and Daisy eating calmly together in the kitchen, their quiet intimacy signaling a restored alliance, while Gatsby remains alone in the moonlight, vigilantly watching the house.

structure.title: VIII
structure.summary: On the dawn after a sleepless night haunted by a foghorn, Nick Carraway rushes to Gatsby’s mansion upon hearing a taxi arrive, finding Gatsby dejected after Daisy briefly appeared at her window before extinguishing the light. Together, they search the dusty, musty rooms for cigarettes, and as they smoke in the dark, Nick Carraway urges Gatsby to flee to Atlantic City or Montreal to evade Tom’s tracing of his car—but Gatsby refuses, clinging to the belief that Daisy never truly loved Tom and will choose him. In a vulnerable recounting, Gatsby reveals how he fell irrevocably in love with Daisy during their youth, deceiving her into believing he had wealth and status, and feeling 'married' to her despite having no real claim to her life. Later, in a reflective moment, Gatsby recalls returning penniless to Louisville after his wedding trip, walking the streets where they once met, and admits he never used his pool all summer. Nick Carraway, unable to leave, misses two trains before departing, shouting that Gatsby is worth more than 'the whole damn bunch put together,' to which Gatsby responds with a radiant, understanding smile. Meanwhile, George Wilson, shattered by Myrtle’s death and convinced the driver of a yellow car murdered her, wanders disoriented through Port Roosevelt and Gad’s Hill, eventually arriving in West Egg and asking for directions to Gatsby’s house. At two o’clock, Gatsby puts on his bathing suit, retrieves a pneumatic mattress from the garage, and goes to the pool, instructing the butler to bring any calls—though he no longer expects one. At dawn, gunfire is heard; Nick Carraway rushes to the scene and finds Gatsby’s body floating on the mattress in the pool, while the gardener discovers Wilson’s corpse nearby, completing the tragedy.

structure.title: IX
structure.summary: Following Gatsby’s death, Nick Carraway is left to navigate the chaotic aftermath as police, photographers, and reporters swarm his mansion, while false narratives shaped by Catherine’s testimony and a detective’s label of Wilson as a 'madman' distort the truth. Desperate to notify Daisy and Meyer Wolfsheim, Nick Carraway receives no response—Wolfsheim’s evasive letter confirms his refusal to attend, and Daisy and Tom have vanished without trace. On the third day, Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives by train from Minnesota, visibly overwhelmed, and shares a photograph of Gatsby’s house and a childhood copy of Hopalong Cassidy containing Gatsby’s self-improvement schedule, revealing the depth of his pride. Despite Nick Carraway’s efforts, nearly all guests refuse to attend the funeral, including Klipspringer, who calls only for his tennis shoes, and Wolfsheim, who avoids it entirely; only Gatz, a Lutheran minister, and servants are present as rain falls. At the cemetery, the man with owl-eyed glasses—whom Nick Carraway recognizes from Gatsby’s library but cannot name—appears unexpectedly, wipes rain from his glasses to view the grave, murmurs 'Amen to that' in response to a quiet blessing, and later laments that no one else came, calling Gatsby 'the poor son-of-a-bitch.' Afterward, Nick Carraway reflects on the Western roots of himself and his circle, their unsuitability for the East, and the haunting distortion of West Egg symbolized by an El Greco-like vision of a drunken woman on a stretcher ignored by passersby. He meets Jordan Baker one last time, confronts her about their broken relationship and her careless driving, and ends it with sorrow, declaring himself too old to deceive himself. He later encounters Tom Buchanan on Fifth Avenue, who admits to telling Wilson that Gatsby owned the car that killed Myrtle, justifying it as necessary, while weeping over dog biscuits left behind in his apartment; Nick Carraway recognizes Tom and Daisy as careless people who destroy lives and retreat into wealth. Finally, alone at night, Nick Carraway walks to Gatsby’s empty house, erases an obscene word scrawled on the steps, wanders to the beach, and meditates on the lost green light and humanity’s futile struggle against time—'So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.'

plot_summary.plot_summary:
In the spring of 1922, Nick Carraway moves to West Egg, New York, seeking opportunity in the bond business and renting a modest home next to the lavish mansion of the mysterious Jay Gatsby. Through his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom—wealthy residents of East Egg—Nick is drawn into a world of excess and moral decay. He learns of Tom’s affair with Myrtle Wilson, wife of a mechanic in the desolate valley of ashes, and is invited to Gatsby’s extravagant parties, where rumors swirl about the host’s origins. Through Jordan Baker, Nick discovers Gatsby’s secret: he bought his mansion solely to be near Daisy, whom he loved five years earlier as a young officer before she married Tom. Gatsby enlists Nick’s help to reunite with Daisy, and their emotional reunion at Nick’s home reveals the depth of Gatsby’s idealized love and the fragility of his dream.

As summer progresses, tensions escalate between Gatsby and Tom, culminating in a dramatic confrontation at the Plaza Hotel where Daisy, under pressure, refuses to renounce her marriage. That same day, Myrtle Wilson is killed by a speeding yellow car—driven by Daisy but owned by Gatsby—and her husband George, misled by Tom into believing Gatsby was both Myrtle’s lover and her killer, descends into grief-fueled madness. Gatsby, steadfast in his devotion, takes the blame for the accident and waits vigilantly outside the Buchanan home, hoping Daisy will choose him. Meanwhile, Nick struggles to connect with the hollow elite around him, growing disillusioned by their carelessness and moral indifference, particularly after learning Jordan Baker cheated in golf and Tom lies with impunity.

After Gatsby is shot and killed by George Wilson—who then takes his own life—Nick tries to organize a proper funeral but is met with silence from Gatsby’s so-called friends and associates. Only Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives, revealing the humble Midwestern roots and relentless self-improvement that shaped Gatsby’s identity. As Nick reflects on the emptiness of the East and the corruption of the American Dream, he confronts Jordan Baker one last time, ending their relationship with sorrow, and later encounters Tom, who coldly admits to directing Wilson to Gatsby. Alone at Gatsby’s abandoned mansion, Nick gazes across the bay at the now-dimmed green light, realizing that Gatsby’s tragedy was not just lost love but the futile human struggle to recapture a past that can never be reclaimed. He departs the East, haunted by the image of boats beating against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.
